SupportsAdaptation pathway: Employer training leaves workers behind

Open topic: Adaptation pathway: Employer training leaves workers behind

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: skills constraints and workforce adaptation through 2030

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report synthesises employers’ expectations about transformation barriers, changing tasks and skills, and workforce responses through 2030. Its 2024 survey evidence emphasises skills shortages, automation alongside augmentation, and investment in training and talent availability. These are reported expectations and plans—not demonstrated effects of AI or endorsements of every policy employers favour. Repeated profile extracts provide comparisons within one source rather than independent views.

Corpus source-specific finding

Skills gaps dominate perceived transformation barriers, but sectors face different additional constraints.

Exact returned source excerpt

4.1 Barriers to transformation Skill gaps in the labour market are the primary report, where skills gaps in the local labour market barrier to business transformation perceived by also topped the transformation barriers, backed Future of Jobs Survey respondents for the 2025- by 60% of executives.

SupportsBusiness transformation: Employer expectations exceed realized change

Open topic: Business transformation: Employer expectations exceed realized change

Corpus framing of this source: Employers expect AI-led transformation alongside substantial workforce and skills change

Corpus synthesis of this source: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 uses employer survey evidence to describe expected business transformation through 2030, with AI and information processing leading globally but considerable variation across industries and geographies. The supplied profiles also report workforce churn, skills disruption and AI-related workforce responses. These are employer expectations and reported practices, not evidence that AI has already caused the projected changes; most profile names are absent from the excerpts.

SupportsEmployer expectations: Collaboration accompanies task automation

Corpus framing of this source: Employer expectations for workforce transformation, skills and talent availability to 2030

Corpus synthesis of this source: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 uses the World Economic Forum’s 2024 employer survey to describe anticipated changes in tasks, skills, staffing and talent availability. It presents automation alongside upskilling, augmentation and recruitment, identifies skills shortages and organisational resistance as constraints, and records employers’ preferred workplace and public-policy responses. These are survey expectations and planned actions, not demonstrated effects of AI or completed labour-market changes.

Corpus source-specific finding

Employers expect predominantly human task delivery to shrink while technology and combined human–technology work expand.

The supplied material primarily reports employers’ expectations and plans, not observed AI-caused job losses or the report’s own policy prescriptions. Many extracts omit profile names or cross page boundaries, limiting attribution of individual figures.

Corpus framing of this source: Employer expectations for 2030: reskilling, automation and uneven occupational change

Corpus synthesis of this source: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 contributes employer-survey evidence on workforce transformation over 2025–2030. It reports plans to combine training, recruitment, automation and redeployment, alongside substantial sectoral and geographic variation. These are expectations and stated intentions, not demonstrated AI-caused employment effects; repeated profile extracts represent the same evidence rather than additional views.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: employer expectations for jobs, skills and workforce adaptation

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report uses employer survey evidence to project workforce change in 2025–2030. It anticipates growing demand for AI-related roles and skills alongside substantial clerical contraction, with variation across industries and economies. It reports employers’ plans for training, hiring, automation and redeployment rather than demonstrating realised AI-driven displacement. Many supplied profile excerpts omit their industry or geographical names, limiting precise attribution.

The findings describe employer expectations, not observed employment outcomes.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: skills constraints and workforce adaptation to 2030

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report synthesises employers’ 2024 survey responses about transformation barriers, changing task allocation and workforce plans to 2030. Its principal finding is that skills gaps constrain transformation more widely than other barriers. The profiles show substantial sectoral and geographical variation, while employers emphasise training, technology, recruitment and workplace reforms. These are reported expectations and intentions, not demonstrated effects or uniformly endorsed policy recommendations.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: employer expectations for skills, automation and workforce transitions

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report synthesises employer survey expectations for 2025–2030, with industry, economy and regional profiles. It presents upskilling, hiring and technological augmentation alongside automation and staff reductions, stresses uneven effects across occupations and locations, and identifies skills and organisational barriers. These are principally reported plans and forecasts, not observed AI-caused employment outcomes or prescriptions endorsed by every respondent.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: employer expectations for changing tasks, skills and workforce strategies

Its economy, region and industry profiles show substantial variation, including contrasting forecasts for lawyers. These are survey-based forecasts and employer plans, not evidence of realised AI displacement.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: employers expect technological change alongside extensive workforce adaptation

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report contributes 2024 employer-survey evidence on expected workforce changes through 2030, rather than measured future outcomes. Its economy, region and industry profiles describe declining predominantly human task shares, substantial training needs, persistent talent constraints and varied policy priorities. It reports employers’ plans and expectations; these do not establish that AI alone causes the projected changes or that preferred interventions will deliver their intended benefits. Many supplied profiles lack identifying headings or contain interleaved table text, limiting attribution of some figures.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: skills constraints and workforce adaptation through 2030

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report uses employer survey evidence to describe anticipated workforce change, barriers to transformation and planned responses. It emphasises reskilling, AI-capable hiring and broader talent pipelines, while distinguishing employers’ expectations from realised outcomes. The supplied profile extracts show substantial variation, but missing headings and interleaved tables limit some sector-specific interpretations.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: skills constraints and workforce adaptation to 2030

Corpus synthesis of this source: The World Economic Forum reports employers’ 2024 expectations for workforce transformation through 2030. Its contribution combines global survey rankings with industry, economy and regional profiles: employers anticipate more technology-delivered work while prioritising training, recruitment and better employment practices. These figures describe perceptions and plans, not demonstrated intervention effects or realised job losses. Many supplied profile excerpts omit geographic names or interleave chart columns, limiting precise attribution.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: skills constraints and workforce adaptation to 2030

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report synthesises employers’ 2024 survey responses about transformation through 2030. It identifies skills gaps as the leading perceived barrier and documents plans for training, automation, augmentation, hiring and broader talent recruitment. Its economy, region and industry profiles show substantial variation. These are employers’ expectations and intended responses, not demonstrated effects of AI or evidence that the proposed measures will succeed.

Corpus framing of this source: Employer expectations for workforce transformation, skills and AI through 2030

Corpus synthesis of this source: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 contributes cross-economy, regional and industry survey evidence on changing tasks, skills needs, transformation barriers and workforce strategies. It reports employers’ expectations and intended responses, rather than demonstrated AI effects or proven policy effectiveness. Many supplied profile extracts omit their geographic or industry headings and interleave chart columns, limiting precise attribution.

Open topic: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: projected workforce restructuring, human–AI collaboration and skills transitions

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report anticipates substantial job creation and displacement through 2030, alongside a shift from predominantly human task delivery towards automation and human–technology collaboration. Its principal evidence is employers’ expectations collected in 2024, combined with ILO employment data; supplementary research from Indeed, LinkedIn and ADP addresses AI capabilities, green hiring and employee preferences. Its legal-sector contribution is narrower: projected legal-secretarial decline, geographically varied lawyer employment forecasts and broader professional-services findings, rather than evidence of observed AI-driven lawyer displacement. Repeated narrative and profile figures are treated as one source. The report recommends targeted training, proactive job transitions and deliberate choices about augmentation versus substitution.

Corpus source-specific finding

The employment outlook is a modelled forecast of macrotrend-driven change, not a measurement of AI-caused job losses.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: employer expectations for technological and workforce transformation

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report supplies 2024 employer-survey evidence on transformation through 2030, comparing economies, regions and industries with global averages. It identifies AI and digital access as major drivers, documents uneven expectations for job reallocation and skill change, and reports employers’ planned training, hiring and inclusion responses. These are expectations and plans, not demonstrated AI effects or legal-sector-specific findings.

Corpus framing of this source: Employers expect skills gaps to constrain transformation and prioritise training through 2030

Corpus synthesis of this source: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 contributes 2024 employer-survey evidence on transformation barriers, changing task allocation, training needs and workforce plans. Its economy, region and industry profiles show substantial variation around global averages. These are employers’ expectations and intended responses, not demonstrated effects of AI or proof that the proposed interventions work; many supplied profile fragments omit names or interleave table columns.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: employer expectations for workforce transformation

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report contributes survey-based comparisons of expected job reallocation, changing skills, AI exposure and workforce responses across economies, regions and industries. It presents employers’ expectations and policy preferences, not demonstrated AI effects or a single prescribed response. The supplied extracts include methodological definitions and historical labour-market context, but many omit profile names or cross page boundaries, limiting attribution.

Corpus framing of this source: Future of Jobs Report 2025: training, automation and talent constraints through 2030

Corpus synthesis of this source: The report uses the World Economic Forum’s 2024 employer survey to describe expected workforce changes through 2030. Its principal contribution is comparative evidence on training needs, human–technology task allocation, transformation barriers and employers’ preferred responses. These figures represent employer expectations and reported plans, not observed future outcomes or proof that particular interventions work. Repeated profile tables report the same survey findings, not independent views; many supplied fragments omit profile names or column headings.
